svg.data-vd-play-label: Play: one action potential, step by step (slowed)
svg.data-vd-steps: [[0, "Resting potential (polarised), about \u221270 mV. The Na\u207a/K\u207a pump uses ATP to move 3 Na\u207a out for every 2 K\u207a in. K\u207a leaks out through K\u207a leak channels, so the inside stays negative. The voltage-gated channels are closed."], [4, "Depolarisation. A stimulus makes the inside less negative. At the threshold (about \u221250 mV) voltage-gated Na\u207a channels open and Na\u207a diffuses in rapidly, opening more channels (positive feedback). The inside becomes positive, about +30 mV."], [7, "Repolarisation. The Na\u207a channels inactivate: the inactivation gate blocks them. Voltage-gated K\u207a channels open and K\u207a diffuses out, so the potential falls back towards \u221270 mV."], [11, "Hyperpolarisation. The K\u207a channels are slow to close, so extra K\u207a leaves and the potential falls below resting (about \u221280 mV). The Na\u207a channels reset. In this refractory period no new action potential can start."], [14, "Back to resting. The K\u207a channels close and the Na\u207a/K\u207a pump and leak channels restore the resting potential. Very few ions moved: the concentrations hardly change, so the axon is ready for the next impulse."]]
svg.title: Resting potential and action potential at the axon membrane
svg.desc: A section of axon membrane with a sodium–potassium pump, potassium leak channel, voltage-gated sodium channel and voltage-gated potassium channel, showing ion movements during the resting potential, depolarisation, repolarisation and hyperpolarisation, with a graph of membrane potential against time.
svg.text: Resting and action potentials: what happens at the membrane
One small patch of axon membrane, highly magnified, with the graph of its potential below. Slowed about ten thousand times.

g.data-info: High concentration of sodium ions (Na⁺), low concentration of potassium ions (K⁺). At rest it is positive relative to the inside.
High concentration of K⁺ and low Na⁺, plus large negatively charged proteins that cannot leave. At rest it is negative relative to the outside.
Ions cannot cross the hydrophobic core of the bilayer: they move only through channel and pump proteins.
Active transport: using energy from ATP, it pumps 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in. This builds up the concentration gradients, and moves more positive charge out than in.
Always open, so the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺. K⁺ diffuses out down its gradient, making the inside more negative: the main cause of the resting potential.
Closed at rest. At the threshold (about −50 mV) its activation gate opens and Na⁺ floods in. About 1 ms later the inactivation gate blocks it; it resets only when the membrane is negative again.
Opens more slowly than the Na⁺ channel, when the membrane has depolarised; K⁺ diffuses out, repolarising it. It is slow to close too, causing hyperpolarisation.

g.text: DEPOLARISING: Na⁺ in, up to +30 mV
time (slowed; a real action potential lasts about 2 ms)

g.data-info: About −70 mV: the inside is negative compared with the outside. Kept by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump and K⁺ leak channels.
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open; Na⁺ diffuses in and the inside becomes positive (up to about +30 mV). The more channels open, the more depolarisation and the more channels open: positive feedback.
Na⁺ channels inactivate and K⁺ channels open; K⁺ diffuses out and the potential falls back towards −70 mV.

K⁺ channels close slowly, so the potential briefly falls below resting (about −80 mV). During this refractory period a new action potential cannot start, so impulses are separate and travel in one direction.
About −50 mV. If a stimulus depolarises the membrane to this level, an action potential always follows, and always reaches the same size (all-or-nothing).

g.text: 2 Depolarisation: Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ in
3 Repolarisation: K⁺ channels open, K⁺ out
4 Hyperpolarisation: K⁺ channels slow to close
5 Back to resting: pump and leak channels
